questions.q: In the example ({case_id: ev_014, baseline_v14: pass, current_v15: fail, status: REGRESSION}), why is this flagged as a regression even if v15's overall pass rate is higher than v14's?
options: It isn't actually a regression if the overall pass rate improved
Regression testing asks whether anything that used to work stopped working, independent of the overall pass rate
The case_id field determines whether something counts as a regression
v15 is always considered worse than v14 by definition
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes overall improvement from regression: a specific case flipping from pass to fail is a regression regardless of what happens to the aggregate pass rate.

questions.q: According to the lesson, how should a full eval suite be re-run when shipping a prompt change?
options: Only the specific case the change targeted needs to be re-checked
Re-running the suite is optional if the developer is confident in the change
Only cases added in the last week need to be re-run
The entire suite should be re-run on every ship, not just cases related to what changed
questions.explain: The lesson states the full suite should be re-run on every ship, since a change can affect behavior on cases that seem unrelated to what was targeted.

questions.q: What does the lesson say should happen when a pass-to-fail flip is detected in the eval suite?
options: It should be treated as blocking, the same way a broken unit test blocks a software deploy
It should be logged but allowed to ship anyway
It should be ignored unless it happens on the same case three times
It should only matter if a human reviewer happens to notice it
questions.explain: The lesson directly compares a regression to a broken unit test: both should block shipping, not be treated as optional follow-up items.

questions.q: In the version history example (v12 through v15 pass rates), what made it possible to identify exactly which version caused the drop?
options: Random guessing among the four most recent versions
Only the final version's score was ever recorded
Each version's prompt text and eval score were both recorded, so the drop could be traced to a specific version
The drop was identified by asking the model which version was worse
questions.explain: Versioning prompts alongside their scores turns a vague 'something regressed recently' into a specific, traceable version — v15 in the example — rather than requiring a guess.

questions.q: What is the key practical difference between "this version scores higher overall" and "this version has no regressions," as the lesson frames it?
options: They are two ways of saying exactly the same thing
A version can score higher overall while still breaking a specific case that used to pass — the two claims require separate checks
Only the overall score matters; individual case results are irrelevant
Regressions can only occur if the overall score drops
questions.explain: The lesson's closing point is that these are distinct claims: an improved aggregate score doesn't guarantee no individual case regressed, so both need to be checked separately.
